etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English dampnen, from Old French damner, from Latin damnāre (“to condemn, inflict loss upon”), from damnum (“loss”).

definitions.definition: (theology, transitive, intransitive) To condemn to hell.
To condemn; to declare guilty; to doom; to adjudge to punishment.

quote.citation: 1599 (first performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Iulius Cæsar”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:
quote.text: He shall not live; look, with a spot I damn him.

quote.citation: 2018 May 12, Stephanie Sinclair, “'What I Learned From Adopting Two Children With Rare Genetic Conditions'”, in Time‎[1]:
quote.text: Lack of access to support services can damn children with disabilities and lesser means to lives where they never harness their full range of abilities.

definitions.definition: To put out of favor; to ruin; to label negatively.
To condemn as unfit, harmful, invalid, immoral or illegal.

quote.citation: 1708 November 8, Alexander Pope, letter to Henry Cromwell
quote.text: You are not so arrant a critic as to damn them [the works of modern poets]  […]  without hearing.

definitions.definition: (sometimes vulgar) To curse; put a curse upon.

quote.citation: c. 1767-1774, Oliver Goldsmith, letter to Mrs. Bunbury
2005, Sonic Team, Sega Studios USA, Shadow the Hedgehog, Sega, PS2, GameCube, Xbox:
quote.text: Where's that damn FOURTH Chaos Emerald!

quote.citation: 1989 December 10, John Zeh, quoting Tony Allen, “AIDS Groups' Execs Arrested In D.C.”, in Gay Community News, volume 17, number 22, page 1:
quote.text: We're  begging, damn near down on our knees, and not getting one red cent.

definitions.definition: (sometimes vulgar) Used to express anger, irritation, disappointment, annoyance, contempt or surprise, etc. See also dammit.
(sometimes vulgar) The word "damn" employed as a curse.
(sometimes vulgar, chiefly in the negative) A small, negligible quantity, being of little value; a whit or jot.
(sometimes vulgar, chiefly in the negative) The smallest amount of concern or consideration.
